barbers.html: Barber shops have been a familiar part of Delano’s business community since the town’s earliest years. By 1881, Reynold M. Bohn was serving local customers, and over the decades barbers including Charles Parnell, Beverly C. Yancey, the Bock brothers, Leslie Krumm, and others operated shops along River Street, Franklin Avenue, and Bridge Avenue. Among the longest-lasting traditions was the Stein family’s barbering business: Armand Stein began working in a barber shop as a boy in 1912, eventually opening his own shop, and his son Fran joined the profession in 1967. When Stein’s Barber Shop moved to Bridge Avenue in 2006, historic fixtures—including an 1800s backbar, 1917 barber chairs, and a hand-cranked barber pole—went with it, preserving a tangible connection to more than a century of Delano barbering history.

1881 – September 15, The Delano Eagle

BARBER – “R. Bohn fills the tonsorial bill for Delano, and his patrons all claim that his work is exceeding good. He has been in Delano since 1879, and came here from Sweden. Delano is well able to support a barber, and Mr. Bohn is never short of custom.”

1885 – January 1, The Delano Eagle

BARBER SHOPS – “Mr. R. Bohn and Mr. Chas. Parnell attend to the tonsorial wants of our citizens; the former’s place of business being on River Street, the latter’s on Franklin Avenue.”

(from the Delano Eagle, August 28, 1890)

“Mr. R. M. Bohn is negotiating for the purchase of I. H. Grafft’s store building on River Street. He intends to use the from room on the lower floor for a hair-dressing room, and the back part of the same story for bath rooms. The upstairs will be remodeled and converted into a photograph gallery by using the glass roof now on the present photograph gallery building which Mr. Bohn intends to convert into a residence. Mr. Bohn made an offer for the building some time ago, but it was not accepted until last week.”

Reynold M. Bohn was born March 4, 1850 in Norway, and immigrated to America in 1879. According to the 1880 census, he was boarding with the Nicholas Begon family on Railroad Avenue in Delano; he was 30 years old, single, and a barber. He married, but his wife committed suicide in 1883. R.M. married Frances A Cebulla on Aug. 23, 1888 in St. Paul. The 1895 census for Delano lists him as a barber and music teacher. In 1900, R.M., his wife Frances, and their four children, Frances Angela, Oscar F., Grover C. L, and Henrietta, were living in Delano; his occupation was listed as barber. R. M. died October 7, 1904, and is buried in the Delano Cemetery. His tombstone is engraved with a musical lyre.

Grover Bohn followed in his father’s footsteps. He began his lifetime career in high school of both barbering and the musical profession, which he followed until his retirement in 1958 after barbering for 49 years. Grover moved to Colorado in 1920, as a veteran to WWI, where he was the assistant band leader of the 358th Infantry Band of the 90th Division.
(Frances A. Bohn married Henry Stein, the brother of Armand Stein, -see below)
(Ads from the Delano Eagle, 1891
Charles Parnell is enumerated on the 1885 Minnesota State Census as living in Delano, with his wife Alice, and their children Laura, Mollie, and Chas.
“The barbers of Delano are Wm. Cowl, Wm. Seippel, Wm. Cuttler, and Wm. Banteon. Now ‘Will” you get shaved.” (from the Delano Eagle, April 5, 1906)

Beverly C. Yancey was a barber in Delano from at least 1895 through 1920. His shop was located on River Street, approximately in the location of the current vacant lot next to Rieder’s Meat Market. B.C. was enumerated either as a black or a mulatto on the census records. In 1895 and 1900 his nephew, Edward Brown was living with him and in 1900 Edward ‘s occupation also was listed as barber.
B.C. Yancy in his shop.

from The Great Northwest Magazine, December 1909:

“If there is any time more than another when a man feels that life is a dream of bliss, it is when he undergoes the soothing manipulation of a first class barber such as Mr. B. C. Yancey, the popular barber, has proven himself to be. Mr. Yancey, though a resident of Delano for more than seventeen years, did not, until last fall, actively unite himself with the business men of Delano. He is established in an up-to-date shop, in size 16x24. Diligent attention and earnest endeavor to steadily grow in his profession has placed him in the lie with many tonsorial artists of a life-long experience. One always finds him in good spirits, happy and jolly. He has become a favorite, as shown by the very large trade he has worked up in so short a period of time. It truly speaks well for the man and his skill in the manipulation of the razor.”

Bock Brothers

Three brothers, Charlie, Emil, and August Bock owned a barber shop together in Delano.

“We have moved from the old barber shop stand into C. M. Conzet’s building where the light will be sufficient to enable us to do first-class work, and we have our shop in first-class shape and ready for business. We have added a bath room to our shop and are ready to serve both ladies and gentlemen with baths. Call and see us in our new quarters. BOCK BROS. (from The Delano Eagle, October 10, 1907)
August Bock, Hamilton in chair; Charlie Bock, Fred Bock in chair; Armand Stein in chair, Carl “Rooster Eckman”, and Eddie Bock.

From the Delano Eagle, 1955:

Charley Bock Has Been Barber for 50 Years

Charley Bock started his barbering with Bev Yancy in June 1905. He had never gone to barber school or served an apprenticeship. His first day in Yancey’s shop he started out by giving shaves and haircuts. “I did a lot of that kind of work for my friends and relatives before I went to work in the shop and I guess Bev thought that was apprenticeship enough”, Charley said.

Charley worked for Yancy for 10 months and then took a job with Billy Cowles for six months. He worked in St. Paul and Billings, Montana before coming back to Delano and buying out the Cowles shop and going into business for himself.

During the time he was barbering in Delano, Charley taught the trade to six barbers: Carl Eckman; Armand Stein; Edward DeNoon; E. H. Bock, a nephew; Milo Bock, his son; and Carl Weldele.
Charley Bock, cutting the hair of Frank Kaeppe. Frank was one of Charley’s first customers when he started barbering in Delano in 1905.

Carl Eckman

The Delano Eagle reported in November of 1909 that Carl Eckman, who had been working in Washington for a few months, would be arriving back in Delano and soon be barbering in W. B. Seippel’s shop. Several years later, in 1925, the Eagle noted that he had moved his shop into the building recently vacated by Lembke’s Economy store on Bridge Street, and that “it was a great improvement over the old one.” (That building is currently the Book Nook.) Carl “Rooster” Eckman worked with Armand Stein for many years.

Armand Stein

Armand was the youngest son of John Louis Stein, an early saloonist in Delano and one of the builders of the brick block building on Bridge Street. “Armand started working in the barber shop in 1912. He was eight years old, and started off by shining shoes and lathering faces for shaves. During World War I, there was a shortage of barbers in Delano, because the majority of the barbers went to work in defense plants for the war effort. Armand’s brother-in-law, Charlie Bock, took him to the governor, and the governor granted the 15-year-old his license.” (from the Delano Eagle, September 11, 2006)

Armand moved out to the west coast in in 1922. After a few years of barbering in California, in San Francisco and Hollywood, Armand returned to Minnesota and opened his shop in Delano.
Armand married Adeline Horsch; their son Francis continued in his father’s business in the same location on River Street.
Fran Stein started barbering with his father Armand in 1967. He went on to barber full-time for fifty-eight years. In 2006 Fran moved his shop to a new location across from the Delano City Hall.

The history of Stein’s Barber Shop did not end when it moved. The backbar, from the 1800s; chairs, bought new in 1917; and the hand-cranked barber pole, only one or two of those types of barber poles left in the country, accompanied Fran on the move.

“Krumm’s Barber and Beauty Shop, located on the corner of Bridge and River Street, Delano, was owned and operated by Mr. and Mrs. Leslie Krumm, who took over the business from Mr. and Mrs. Ed Bock in 1941. For nine years, before coming to Delano, Mr. and Mrs. Krumm operated a barber and shop at 5460 Nicollet Ave., Minneapolis.” (from the 1946 The Eagle presents Delano, Minnesota)

The shop was in the same building where the Bock Brother barbered in 1907.
Mr. Leslie Krumm daughter Ihla Rae; Mrs. Krumm with customer, 1946

Dennis Kettenacker opened a barber shop in that same building in 1961. He was killed in a car-train crash in 1966, and Lowell McKinley bought the shop in 1967. He eventually sold it and went on to work in Excelsior, Maple Plain, and Victoria, before coming back to Delano. In 2022 Lowell McKinley joined Fran working out of Stein’s Barber Shop on Bridge Avenue. Lowell and Fran had known each other since 1966, but this was the first time they worked together. Fran sold his shop in 2025, and it the new owners opened Wright Cuts.

bakeries.html: Bakeries have been a familiar part of Delano’s business community for well over a century. One of the earliest was operated by Napoleon Hamel, who moved to Delano in 1902 and became known for a modern, well-equipped bakery offering breads, cakes, pies, pastries, and other baked goods, some of which were shipped to neighboring communities. He continued in the bakery business until his death in 1927. Other bakeries followed, including the Delano Home Town Bakery, Palm’s Bakery, and Roy and Mrs. Hanson’s bakery, which by 1946 was Delano’s only retail bakery. Perhaps the best remembered was the Delano Bakery, opened by Kerney and Genevieve Jacobson in 1948. For nearly 40 years, the couple produced countless loaves of bread, hundreds of thousands of doughnuts, and thousands of decorated cakes, building a loyal following that extended well beyond Delano. The original bakery closed in 1988, but the Delano Bakery name continued in a new location—almost on the same site where Napoleon Hamel had operated his bakery generations earlier.

(from The Great Northwestern Magazine, December 1909)

Napoleon Hamel “We believe that no town of the size of Delano can boast of a cleaner, more attractive and more modern bakery than you have right here. People who are acquainted with Napoleon Hamel and who have occasion to patronize him always remark that his place is one of the cleanest, most inviting and up to date that they have seen. Besides this the store and shop are large and finely equipped and only the best of goods are handled. Mr. Hamel has been established here for the past seven years, although he has had much more experience in this line, and during that time he has always met the demands of the public in the most satisfactory manner. He carries an excellent stock of the choicest cakes, pies, pastries, rolls and baker’s goods of every variety. He ships goods of this nature to Watertown, Waverly and Montrose. He is prompt and courteous in attending to his patrons, and employs only the most competent and obliging help. He is a man of honest convictions, more than ordinary discernment and business enterprise and sagacity.”

(from the History of Wright County Minnesota Volume II 1915)

The brief business directory lists Napoleon Hamel, baker.

Napoleon Hamel was born in Quebec, Canada in 1872; he immigrated to the United States and Minnesota in 1886. The Minneapolis City Directories for 1890 and 1891 list Napoleon as a cook in the French Hotel. Napoleon was working as a cook in Minneapolis in the 1895 census. The Minneapolis Directories for 1899 and 1900 show that he was in the restaurant business at 1009 Washington Avenue N. Napoleon married Virginia Scott on August 23, 1897, in Hennepin County. The couple moved to Delano in 1902, and the 1905 census lists Napoleon as a baker. He continued to have a bakery in Delano until he passed away September 23, 1927. Napoleon and Virginia had four children: Bernadette Angela, Pearl Alice, Marie Eugenie, and Joseph Napoleon. Bernadette married Edward Henry Dunn; their daughter Virginia married Clarence “Buzz” Matter. Pearl married Alvin C Weihe in 1936. Marie married Francis Harney, and Joseph married Mary T. Kelly. Napoleon’s wife Virginia passed away in 1925; she and Napoleon are buried in Calvary Cemetery in Delano.
The Delano Home Town Bakery opened in September 1930, next to the (old) City Hall. Swanberg and Cox, proprietors.
This ad appeared in the Delano Eagle in April 1933.

(from the Special Edition - The Eagle, 1946)

“Mr. and Mrs. Roy Hanson have operated for the past 15 years. Starting on Third Street in 1933, after a few months they moved downtown where they have since been located. Presently the bakery is situated next door to Marshall-wells store. It is currently the only retail bakery in Delano.”
This building is the Ziebarth/Lebovsky Block. It currently houses, in 2026, DownTown Social. Hanson’s Bakery was in the south half of the building.
New Delano Bakery Will Be Ready for Business Saturday

“The new Delano bakery next to the city hall will open for business on Saturday, May 8, according to the owner, Mr. Hilmer Hansen. Mr. Hansen, who came here from Hutchinson where he had been operating a bakery for his father, has had many years’ experience in the bakery business. Something a little different in the line of bakery goods will be offered in the Danish Kringle. This according to Mr. Hansen, looks like a giant pretzel but is a form of coffee cake.”
The building next to city hall was a bakery for several years, with several different proprietors, but became a Red Owl store in 1940.
Kerney and Genevieve Jacobson opened the Delano Bakery in 1948.

Cornelius ("Kerney") and Genevieve Jacobson first opened the original Delano Bakery in 1948.  Kerney was a cook in the army during World War II, and upon returning from the war, he and his wife, Gen, along with their 4-year-old son, Dale, opened the famous “Delano Bakery” in Delano, Minnesota.  

The bakery quickly became very successful, and for the next 40 years, Kerney and Gen made countless loaves of bread for all the schools in the area, hundreds of thousands of doughnuts for all their regular customers from locals to non-locals, and thousands of beautifully decorated cakes for graduations, birthdays, and especially weddings.   Kerney would do all the baking and Genevieve would decorate as many as 15+ wedding cakes in a single weekend.  In over 40 years, neither of them missed a single day of work.   They stayed very busy and the bakery only continued to become more well known and well-respected.  Genevieve remembers the day she realized they had baked over one million loaves of bread.

The original Delano Bakery remained open for almost 40 years before finally closing its doors in 1988, when Dale and his family moved from Delano to Forest Lake, Minnesota. (historical information from www.thedelanobakery.com)

The Delano Bakery was located on the corner of Bridge Avenue and Second Street. The small pocket park, next to Joe McDonald’s Photography Studio. (The Delano Bakery is the two-story building with the outside staircase in the left of this 1963 photo.)

When the Delano Bakery closed on the corner of Bridge and Second, it opened in a new building around the corner, between Bridge and Railroad avenues. Interestingly, that was almost in the same location where Napoleon Hamel had his bakery.

beck-building.html: The Beck Building at 136 Bridge Avenue E., built by John M. Beck in 1912 next to Delano’s original City Hall, has housed an unusually diverse collection of businesses during its more than century-long history. Beck, a music teacher and director of the Delano Band, originally used the building for his music and stationery business, while his daughter Clotildis “Claudia” Beck operated a photography studio there and created an important visual record of early Delano. Later occupants included the Delano Granite and Marble Works, several bakeries, the Red Owl grocery store, Ditty Plumbing and Heating, and the Delano Family Dental Clinic. Cutting Edge Construction moved into the historic building in 2005, and portions of the early construction added by monument maker Bert Gilmer can still be seen at the rear. In 2026, the storefront was occupied by Western Creations, continuing the Beck Building’s long tradition of adapting to the changing businesses of downtown Delano.
John M. Beck built the building next to the original city hall in 1912.  Over the years it has held many businesses.

J. M. Beck was a music teacher, and served as the director of the Delano Band, as well as directing the choir of St, Peter’s church during the years the family lived in Delano. He built the store for his music and stationary business.
John M Beck, was the director of the Military Band, is in the center of the front row.
His daughter, Clotildis (Claudia) Beck, also had a photography studio in the building.​

beck-building.label: Clotildis B Beck, Woman Photographer in Early Delano

beck-building.html: 1919 - The building is now housing the Delano Granite and Marble Works.​

Bert Gilmer opened a monument shop in Delano in 1917, and bought the building in 1919. He added a tower to the back of the building to handle the pieces of granite. When Clarence Dunn joined the firm in 1925, the Delano Granite offices were still in the building next to the city hall on Bridge Avenue.  He reminisced about looking out the only window in the place - right into the jail next door.

In September of 1930, Mr. H. Swanberg of Chicago and Mr. Cox rented the Bert Gilmer building next to city hall and re-arranged the interior for the manufacture and sale of bakery products. It was promoted as a new business industry for Delano.
The building continued to be a bakery:
The Red Owl Agency was in the building next to the City Hall in 1940, operated by William Kirsch. When he died in April of that year, his wife, Ella, sold the business to Lawrence and Alice Karl.
Mr. and Mrs. Karl operated the Red Owl store for six years, and then sold it to Raymond C. Trueman.  Mr.Trueman died in 1952.
Ditty Plumbing and Heating was located in the building the 60’s.
Ditty Plumbing and Heating was located in the building the 60’s.

Beginning in 1987, Tom Madden, opened his dentistry office in this building.  In 1988 his brother Mark joined him.  They remained at this address until 2004, when they built a new office on Elm Avenue by Delano Public Schools.

In 2005 Cutting Edge Construction, moved to Delano and into the Beck building. Michael Anastasia, who was joined in 1991 by his brother Pete, started the company in 1985 in Long Lake. The business has completed hundreds of commercial restaurant and bar projects and a variety of projects for retailers, service firms, and non-profit organizations, including a number of projects involving historical building and renovation in historical districts in the Minnesota area. Pete Anastasia is the current president of the company and owner of this historical building in Delano, where it is still possible to see some of the original construction added by Bert Gilmer in the back of the building.
Western Creations was in the building in March of 2026, and in September of the same year it transitioned to …….

brick-block-on-bridge.html: Built in 1905 on Bridge Avenue, Delano’s Brick Block Building was an ambitious two-story brick commercial building created by Olof Peterson, Louis and Henry Bock, and John L. Stein. Its 100-foot frontage was divided among Peterson’s shoe store, Stein’s business, and a large center section intended for a department store. Before construction was even complete, the center became a gathering place for plays, dances, and community events and later housed businesses and institutions ranging from Kelly & Murray’s department store and the Delano Café to the post office, Picus clothing store, and Rainbow Inn. Over the decades, other portions of the block were home to Heinen Hardware, the Comet Theater, Boyce Funeral Home, Jack’s Food Guild, and the Coast-to-Coast Store, illustrating the building’s central role in generations of Delano commerce and community life. By 2019, the historic building had entered another chapter with The Refoundry and the newly remodeled Jerome Event Center, continuing the Brick Block’s more than century-long presence in downtown Delano.

A handsome business building was erected on Bridge avenue in 1905 by Olaf Peterson, Louis and Henry Bock, and John L. Stein. The plans were drafted by Swan Erickson and called for a solid brick structure with a 100-foot front, 90 feet deep, full basement, plate front, two stories above ground, heating plant for the entire building and all modern conveniences. Mr. Peterson’s shoe store would occupy the east 25x90 end, John Stein’s business the west 25x90 end, and the center room, 50x90, would be rented for a department store.

Five brick masons and five tenders began laying the brick in June of 1905; the work went fast, finishing in eight months!

Ole Peterson occupied his section (the east end) of the new building beginning in September 1905. Mr. Peterson was a shoemaker. He was born in Sweden, where he learned his trade until 25 years of age. He emigrated to the United States and moved to Delano in December of 1869. Mr. Peterson was still listed as the owner of a retail shoe store in Delano on the 1910 census. It was said he carried one of the most extensive lines of boots and shoes found outside of the larger cities.

Peterson’s remaining stock was sold out in 1913; He died January 17, 1914. Berner Blomquist moved his furniture store into Ole’s Bockman’s building, which was Ole Peterson’s building after adding a balcony to accommodate part of his stock. (Ole Bockman was Ole Peterson’s son-in-law)

Heinen Hardware moved into this location in 1933 and remained there until it closed in 1991.

Kevin Lindquist then bought the building and opened a custom framing store. The building later was the home of Delano Floral and Gifts, followed by a school spirit wear business for Delano and surrounding districts. The Refoundry opened in the building in 2019.The building was sold in 2025, and currently is the home of The Vintage Storyteller.

The center section of the brick block belonged to the Bocks. Although the entire building was not completed, it was secured by the Dramatic Club for its grand production of “The Deserter” for the Fourth of July of 1905. A large stage was erected, and the site was wired for electric lights.

The space seems to have been used as an center for about the first year and a half. A grand ball was held in October of 1905, with the crowd enjoying the hard maple floor, large room and first-class accommodations.

A masquerade ball in Bock’s building on February 21, 1906, was described as one of the best Delano had ever seen… “the magnificent hall was brilliantly lighted and beautifully decorated, with gaily dressed masqueraders winding in and out through the giddy maze.”

Finally, Kelly & Murray, of Waverly, rented Bock’s store building in January of 1907. They opened their large general merchandise store in March. L.R. Kelly bought out Kelly & Murray in 1910, and then in 1913 closed the store and sold out all the remaining merchandise.
The second-floor space was used for offices and living quarters.
In 1917 the center of the brick block building housed the post office, with Henry J. Bock as the postmaster, and a restaurant, the Delano Café.

Wm. Picus bought the Bock building in 1921 in the section that had been the Delano Café and opened a department store. The American Legion located their club rooms above Picus’ store in 1928. Vennett Beauty Shop was located over the Picus store when the American Legion moved. Angie’s Beauty Shop was located on the street level from 1937-1943, succeeded by Mella-Dor Beauty Box., and Then Kitty’s Beauty Shop until 1948.

In 1957 Ed and Marge Andres and their children moved to Delano, and opened a Coast-to-Coast.

Store . Son Jerome, having completed four years in the U. S. Navy, entered the business with his parents in 1971. Jerome owned and expanded the store until 2005, when it was bought by Chris Johnson who moved the business out to Highway 12.

The Rainbow Inn was in the center of the brick block in 1946, next to Heinen Hardware. It was owned and operated by Robert Nicolai and Mr. and Mrs. Everett Zabel. Serving beer, soft drinks and refreshments, it was a popular spot for light lunches. The Rainbow was later operated by Bud and Colleen DeMaris. The Rainbow Inn section of the Brick Block was later part of the Coast to Coast store.

The fourth section (the west end) of the brick block was built by John L. Stein, who died in October of 1906, soon after the building was completed. His wife Josephine inherited the building, and the contents of a saloon. The Comet Theater, run by his son-in-law Ed Probst, was in that location for several years. The Boyce Funeral Home occupied the site just before Jack Schumacher bought the building from the Stein estate in 1941, remodeled the front and moved his Jack Sprat store there.

east-brick-block-on-bridge.html: The east end of Delano’s Brick Block at 137 Bridge Avenue E. has served the community through more than a century of changing businesses. Built in 1905 by Olof Peterson in partnership with Henry and Louis Bock and John L. Stein, the property’s early history was connected to Peterson’s shoe store and later to several furniture businesses. In 1933, William Heinen moved his hardware store into the building, where Heinen Hardware remained for 58 years, until 1991. The building later housed Kevin Linquist’s custom framing shop, and its upstairs apartment even appeared as a filming location in the 1998 movie A Simple Plan. More recent occupants have included Delano Floral and Gifts and The Refoundry. After another sale and the naming of the building as the Delano Brick Block, The Vintage Storyteller opened there in May 2026, continuing the building’s long tradition as a downtown Delano business location.

The Brick Block building on Bridge Avenue was built in 1905 by Olof Peterson in conjunction with Henry and Louis Bock and John L. Stein. Olof Peterson had come to Crow River (Delano) in 1869 and opened a shoe store. His business, from at least 1894, was just to the east of the brick block. Olof retired in 1913 and died in 1914; his building went to his son-in-law, Ole Backman.
Berner Bloomquist moved his furniture business into that space in March 1917, adding additional space by erecting a balcony.

In 1919 John Berlin tore out the west wall of the old shoe store stand and connected it to his present store in the brick block.

John Lohmiller had a furniture store in the building until September 1933, when the building was sold.

In 1933 William Heinen moved his hardware store from River Street to the east end of the brick block building. Heinen Hardware remained there for 58 years, until 1991.

Kevin Linquist bought the building and opened a custom framing shop.

The apartment upstairs was used for Bill Bob Thornton’s character’s apartment in the 1998 movie “A Simple Plan.”

Delano Floral and Gifts was in the building from 2000-2015

From 2019 to 2025, The Refoundry, a store specializing in repurposed furniture and home accessories, occupied the building. The building was again sold and was named the Delano Brick Block. In May 2026 the Vintage Storyteller opened in that location.

eppel-building.html: The Eppel Building at 100 Bridge Avenue E., at the corner of Bridge Avenue and River Street, is one of Delano’s oldest surviving commercial landmarks. Its history reaches back to 1871, when Charles Eppel moved the building from south of the railroad tracks to its present location and opened a mercantile store selling dry goods and groceries along with a saloon. The building had also been the Eppel family home, where the first Catholic Mass in the community was celebrated by a missionary priest. Over the years, additions were made and the property housed a harness shop and an early restaurant operated by Charles’s son Leo. During much of the 20th century, the building became closely associated with Curley’s Men’s Clothing Store, later operated by Marshall Dainsberg and then Carroll Lundeen. Since the clothing store closed, numerous businesses have occupied the building, including Linnea’s Ice Cream Parlor, Curves for Women, Cyber Geeks, Bridge House Coffee & Café and Nature Nook Cafe and Wine Bar. Although its exterior has been extensively remodeled, the building retains its original form and remains recognizable as the structure Charles Eppel moved to this prominent downtown corner more than 150 years ago.

• This building at 100 Bridge Ave. E. was originally located near the present site of St. Peter's church. It was the home of Charles Eppel and his family.

  • The first mass in the town was read by a missionary priest in this house.

  • In 1871, Charles moved his building to its present location and opened a mercantile store and saloon. Additions were made to accommodate a harness shop.

• Charles' son, Leo opened his first restaurant in the back room of the saloon.

  • In the early 20th century the Eppel building became Curley's Clothing Store. It was sold to Carroll Lundeen and became Lundeen's.
In 1998 the building was used during the filming of “A Simple Plan” staring Bill Paxton, Billy Bob Thornton and Bridget Fonda.

Several businesses have occupied the building, including a China and Crystal business, Linnea's Ice Cream Parlor, Curves for Women, Cyber Geeks, Wilbur’s Coffee and currently Nature Nook Cafe and Wine Bar.

hollywood-in-delano-and-local-talent.html: A Simple Plan

Hollywood invaded Delano in 1998 as the film, “A Simple Plan,” starring Billy Bob Thornton, Bill Paxton, Bridget Fonda, and Laura Dern, was shot in and around the village. Filming was set to begin January 2, but due to a lack of snow the crew was forced to go to Ashland, Wisconsin to film exterior scenes. Parts of the film were also shot in Camp Ihduhapi in Loretto, and at the Moravian church near Victoria, MN.

There were about 65 small Midwestern towns that were being considered as locations for the film, but Delano’s proximity to the Twin Cities helped its being chosen as the location.

Filming in Delano began January 19. Buildings in downtown Delano were given a facelift to create Tippy’s Town Tavern, the Foss Funeral Home, and the Delano Feed and Grain Mill. The Public Library (the Old City Hall) appeared as the Wright County Annex Building, with the interior of the second floor serving as the police station.

The crew came back to Delano in February to reshoot several scenes that had been lost in transport. The Delano Public Works Department had to put snow back on the street, and the city agreed to keep the Christmas decorations up longer than usual because the film takes place around Christmas.
Several residents were cast as extras, and older local cars and trucks from the 70’s and 80’s, rusty and dirty, were requested for the film.
“Area people who appeared as extras in the funeral scene included Laura Murphy, K. J. McDonald, Joe McDonald (as the hearse driver), Dan Reiner, Jerome Andres and Randall Gerhart.”
The film opened in area theaters Friday, January 22, 1999, giving Delano residents the opportunity to see their city on the big screen.
Butch Automatic and the Four Speeds
Popular Local Rock Group

1974 photo

Bob Seliski, Bob Hutter, Dale Graunke, Mike Mathisen, Dave Socher, Brad Bruhn, Dave Pawelk

Butch Automatic and the Four Speeds was formed in 1974 by friends from Delano and Watertown high schools and quickly became one of central and southern Minnesota’s premier rock groups. When Butch Automatic began, its members were music-loving teenagers who looked up to groups like White Sidewalls, The Rockin’ Hollywoods, and Travelin Band Grease Band.

The band’s first members included Bob Hutter, Dave Socher, Mike Mathisen, Bob Seliski, Dale Graunke, Dave Pawelk, and Brad Bruhn. Bob Seliski’s brother, Joe Seliski, joined soon after the band’s start, and vocalist Doreen Shrode was added in the 1990s.

“Butch Automatic was a group of regular guys – with below to average musical talents – who took an idea and worked very hard to create a musical experience that appealed to their audience,” said Joe Seliski in an interview in the Delano Herald Journal, September 3, 2013. “The group added an energy to the music that was not present with other groups.” Dale Graunke added “We were always a theatrical band.”

Butch Automatic has entertained well over half a million people since its inception in 1974, including performing with national acts such as the Monkees, the Trashmen, Tommy and the Shondells, and the Ventures.
Delano Community Theater

The extravagant comedy, “The Womanless Wedding,” was presented January 23 and 24, 1928, in the new high school auditorium, sponsored by the Delano American Legion. Eighty local business and professional men played all the roles. It was reported in the Delano Eagle that “if Delano business institutions suffered a decline for a few days, it was because the proprietors were taking time off to discuss the latest styles in feather fans, high-heeled slippers and evening gowns.” Following the presentation of the rollicking farce, the Eagle stated that the town had been “scoured in search of high-heeled pumps, slippers, party dresses, hats and lingerie to fit the staid businessmen, who blossomed forth as stately matrons, vampires, fashions plates, flappers and country maids.” The play was a huge success, with the performances attended by about 1300 people.

“The Womanless Wedding” was again presented in Delano January 15, 1943, this time sponsored by the Delano Sportsmen’s Club. All of the proceeds from the show were set aside in a Soldiers Homecoming Fund, to give the boys in service a celebration when they returned in victory. Parts of the play were updated to reflect the current times, including ‘Sally Rand,” “Kate Smith.” “Sophie Tucker,” Eleanor Roosevelt,” “Shirley Temple,” “Carmen Miranda,” “Gypsy Rose Lee” and other well-known celebrities as well as the essential bride and groom. It was difficult to tell if the cast or the audience had more fun; Edward Leiter, the ring bearer, carried a ring of Rieder and Schilling’s best bologna on a soft cushion.

Beginning in 1888, Delano residents crowded the village hall to be entertained by traveling theatricals and home talent plays.

In 1971 the old meeting room above the city offices was once again the center of local theatrical farce. That summer the melodrama “Deadwood Dick” was presented, sponsored by the Delano Recreation Department.
It was complete with olios, house rules and a backdrop of hometown advertising.
Directors were Bill and Sandy Horeis.
Presented three days, August 20-22, Sunday’s standing room only audience included Senator Hubert Humphrey.

The Delano Community Education play in 1988 was “Fools,” featuring Becky Iverson, Tina Gray, Brian Delger, Mark Lewis, Dennis Johnston, Chris Koch, Jim Schmidt, Kathy Hegna, Jackie Johnston, and Ken Schiller.

Barb Roy directed the Delano Community Theater production of M*A*S*H in 1989. Some of the cast members were Rick Workman as Father Mulcahy, Al Holimotz as Klinger, Jim Schmidt as Hawkeye, Scott Shoutz as Trapper John, Dennis Johnston as Col. Blake, Dale Weiman as Radar, Becky Iverson as Hot Lips, and Ken Schiller as Duke Forrest.
Jason Schmidt, Becky Iverson, Jim Schmidt, Ken Schiller, and Melissa Windsperger.
Current dramatic group is the Delano Dramatic Company
Delano Community Bands
Delano has always had interest in having a community band. As early as the summer of 1872, a subscription of $50.00 made possible the organization of the “Delano Cornet Band.”
Delano Cornet Band, date unknown

References to the band were made in the Delano Eagle from then through the next several decades.

*In 1874, the Delano Eagle reported that “in the evening, the band having returned from Buffalo, a lively and happy dance was kept up in Lucas Hall until the witching hour of twelve marked the closing of the Nation’s anniversary.”

*The band went to Charles Eppel’s house to celebrate his 55th birthday in 1891: “The Delano Cornet Band was present in uniform and gave the host the first hint of what was going on by striking up a lively air in front of the house.”

*Prof. R. M. Bohn (also a local barber) retired in 1893 from directing the band for several years He was presented a special plaque by the members of the Cornet band in appreciation for his work.
Fourth of July parade, Railroad Avenue in Delano, ca. 1896. “The parade was led by the Delano Cornet Band in their immaculately new white uniforms.”

The band took part in parades, gave concerts, and traveled to other communities to perform.

*In 1896 the Delano Cornet Band was engaged to attend the first celebration of Holy Mass by Rev. Otto Zachman at St. Michael’s church.

But apparently, the band was not always organized. An article in 1908 Eagle stated that Delano needs “a good band, the material is here but only lacking organization.”

In 1921, C.G. Roosen reminisced that “the Delano Cornet Band was a large asset in the social life of the village for many years and with all the good organizations in that line which we have had since – there has never been one better.”

In 1912 the band was called the Delano Military Band. It played at the ground-breaking for the new St. Peter’s Church, and for its dedication in 1913.

Standing: Charles Carlson, Charles Lohmiller, Frank Yantes, Simon Loch, Sam Ash, Chester Orrison, Carl Weddele, Matt Bernick, Jack Lohmiller

Seated: Herbert Probst, Charles Wood, Pete Peterson, Oscar Hildebrandt, Prof. Beck, Frank Schaffer, C. T. Buckley, Rastey Yantes.
Conductor Professor John Beck

There was a bandstand on Railroad Avenue for concerts, that was later moved to Central Park.

The Delano Military Band gave a concert in the new bandstand on August 5, 1915, and every two weeks thereafter.
Unknown name or date or this band in the bandstand.

This is the Delano Band in the late 1920’s, under the leadership of Alvin Weihe. This group played at surrounding towns, and at all the picnics, parades, and celebrations. They also played a day at the State Fair. The band practiced upstairs in the city hall every Monday evening. Alvin Weihe is standing behind the bass drum in the right.

The community band also occasionally played at the local baseball games. During the 1928 tournament the Delano band furnished music during the morning and afternoon games, as noted by the Delano Eagle.

The current Delano Community Band is an inter-generational, all-volunteer concert band. Established in November 2017, band membership has comprised of musicians ranging from strong high school students to those who’ve been performing for over 50 years. This diversity of experience enables the band to offer growth as well as performance opportunities for area musicians. They rehearse for about 90 minutes on Thursday evenings at 7:00p.m. in the Delano High School band room. Their repertoire spans virtually every major genre of western music from traditional concert band fare to renditions of early music, to adaptations of orchestral pieces, to contemporary iterations of popular music and modern works for band.

lebovsky-building.html: The Lebovsky Building at 141 Bridge Avenue E. has been part of Delano’s commercial history since at least 1894, when Olof Peterson operated a boot and shoe store there. Over the following decades, the building housed an assortment of businesses, including the Columbia Clothing Store, shoe and clothing stores operated by the Berlin family and others, a Marshall-Wells associate store, and William Heinen’s hardware business. In 1940, Lebovsky’s Store, a family business founded by Thomas S. Lebovsky on River Street in 1906, moved to the Bridge Street location. The Lebovsky family continued the store for more than four decades, making it a familiar fixture in downtown Delano until it closed in 1984. Since then, the building has been home to Calico Cat Fabrics, the Crow River News, Dwayne’s Games, and Bridge Avenue Ceramics. In 1994, Joe McDonald moved his photography business into the building, beginning another long chapter in the history of this enduring downtown storefront.

The building at 141 Bridge Ave. can be traced back a far as 1894, and perhaps even earlier. In 1894 it was a boot and shoe store, owned by Olof Peterson.

In 1905 Mr. Peterson, in conjunction with Louis and Henry Bock and John Stein built the Brick Block Building on Bridge, adjacent to his shoe store. Ole moved next door and occupied his new store. The Delano Eagle reported that his former building was rented by to the Schmidt Bros., of Belle Plain, who bought and shipped poultry, butter, and eggs.

In 1909 Ole Peterson put an addition on his old store and raised the ceiling.
The Columbia Clothing Store was in the building ca. 1913.

It seems likely that Ole Peterson sold his business and buildings to John Berlin, who was also in the shoe business.

In 1919 John Berlin tore out the west wall of his former shoe store and connected the building to his present adjoining store. In December of that same year, O.C. Damsberg opened his Clothing & Gents Furnishing Emporium in the Berlin Building. Damsberg was a tailor, and became known as “Curley the Tailor”
Jasper Berlin, son of John, opened a shoe store in the old stand in 1922. He sold out to Homer F. Ehle in 1926. Ehle had a bankruptcy sale at the end of the year.

In 1936 Robert Gamble opened a new store in the building across from the Delano City Hall, a M.W. Associate Store. The Marshall-Wells Store remained there until 1939.

William Heinen moved his hardware store into the east end of the Brick Block, Ole Petersen’s space, in 1933. It was connected to the building adjoining to the east.

In 1940 Lebovsky’s moved from their store on River Street to their new location on Bridge Street in the Heinen building, across from City Hall.

Lebovsky’s original store was built and opened on River Street in 1906 by Thomas S. Lebovsky. When Thomas passed away in 1932, his wife, Mary, continued the business, with the assistance of her son Richard and daughter Ruth. The store was taken over in 1942 by sons Frank and Richard. Richard came from Minneapolis, and Richard recently returned from the service. Frank and his wife Winnifred worked at the family store between 1944 and 1955. Richard and his wife, Madeline “Maggie” Alger, then continued as the proprietors the Lebovsky Store.
Bridge Street, 1970’s Lebovsky’s on the left side.

Lebovsky’s Store closed in 1984 and was sold to Lola Pool, who opened

the Calico Cat Fabrics Store with her co-owner Shirley Krueger.

In 1989 the Crow River News office was in the building, followed by Dwayne’s Games, and from 1991-1993 it was Bridge Avenue Ceramics

Joe McDonald moved into the building in 1994, and it has been the McDonald Photography Studio since then.

longish-building.html: Built in 1904 by bricklayer and stonemason John Longosh, the Longosh Building has been part of Delano’s Bridge Avenue streetscape for more than 120 years. Longosh, a German immigrant who arrived in Delano in the 1870s, constructed the two-story brick building with commercial space below and living quarters above. The Longosh Building SoCT Over the decades, the building housed an assortment of businesses, including a saloon, barber shop, Curley’s clothing store, a harness and leather shop, and Bill’s Shoe Repair. The Longosh Building SoCT Its long history reflects the changing businesses and everyday life of downtown Delano. Today, in 2026, the historic building continues its commercial role as the home of Vintage on Bridge and the Book Nook.

John Longosh was born in Upper Silesia, Germany in 1848, emigrated to the United States in 1872, coming directly to St. Paul, and then came to Delano about a year later. He was by trade a bricklayer and stonemason and built more than one building in Delano.

May 1904 - “John Longosh is getting the material on the ground for the erection of a solid brick building, 24x40, which he will build on his lot on the south side of Bridge Street. It will be a two-story structure, the first floor fitted up for a store and the second floor fixed for living rooms.”

April 9, 1908 – “John Longosh is tearing down his old frame building on Bridge Street and will erect in its place a solid brick structure, 22 x 40.” (on the north side of Bridge Street)

Nov. 4, 1909 – M. P. Berneck is now nicely settled in his new quarters in the John Longosh building on Bridge Street.”
The Longosh building, next to the State Bank of Delano.

1933 - “The Longosh building next to the State Bank of Delano is being renovated and painted and will be the future home of Curley’s Men’s Furnishing store. Curley told the editor he expected to be nicely settled in his new location by the end of next week.”

May 4, 1933 – Curley the Tailor moved next door to the State Bank of Delano.

1936 – “In the fall of 1936 Dr. Guilfoile came to Delano and established his medical practice with offices over what was then Carl Eckman’s barber shop, (Bill’s Shoe Repair in 1979).”

Oct. 7, 1937 – Curley’s and Peters Change Locations.

“Beginning Monday Curley’s clothing store will be located in the building now occupied by Peter’s harness shop, and the harness shop will move into Curley’s present location. Mr. Peter’s bought the building now occupied by Eckman’s barber shop, Dr. Guilfoile, and Curley some time ago. He has made his living quarters above the clothing store and will now move his business over there also. In order that all his customers get quickly acquainted with his new location Bud Dainsberg is advertising a weeklong sale to be held in his new location starting Monday.”
Mr. Peter’s sold his harness and leather shop to Claus and Lillian Eckhoff. In about 1942.

The business was bought by Bill Benson in 1973, who had Bill’s Shoe Repair.

The Longosh building on the south side of Bridge Avenue has been a saloon, a barbershop, a clothing store, a harness and leather shop, and a shoe repair shop. Today, in 2026, it is the home of Vintage on Bridge and the Book Nook.

state-bank-of-delano-bldg.html:
• 1908: The State Bank of Delano was incorporated.

  • 1910: The State Bank of Delano and the Wright County Bank was consolidated.

Interior view of State Bank Delano on Bridge Avenue circa 1912. Seated behind the desk is Charles McDonald and standing is Louis Probst. The customer is Reverend Hilding Eagle. The First bank president was Henry C. Bull.

1908: State Bank of Delano with white enamel brick front. The main banking room had a tile floor, an Italian marble wainscoting, with verde-antique base and rail. The fixtures were the best quarter sawed oak, with oxidized copper grillwork and every convenience for the conduct of business. The vault door was a massive Victor and gave a finish to the counting room, which was most striking. With its steel ceiling and walls was insured cleanliness, to say nothing of the pleasing effect. But decoration alone were not sought, the bank being supplied with a Victor safe which made losses by burglary impossible. Hot water was used for heating and electricity or lighting. The interior equipment was undoubtedly the most artistic and best in point of quality of any bank of its size in the state. In addition to general banking business this house wrote insurance in many of the vest companies and handled real estate. (as described The Great Northwest Magazine, December 1909).

• 1975: The State Bank of Delano moved to a new location on Railroad Ave (now the Delano Great Rivers Public Library).

  • 1988: The building was occupied by Flowers by Styve

  • 2000: The building was occupied by Bridge Floral

  • 2002: The State Bank of Delano moved to a new location on Highway 12

  • The building has been faithfully restored by the office of MacLean Law Office.
The old bank vault is now 'the most secure bathroom in Delano'.

west-brick-block-on-bridge.html: The west end of Delano’s Brick Block has been home to a remarkable variety of businesses and community services since the building was constructed in 1905. J. L. Stein developed this portion of the block on the site of an old blacksmith shop, with the Northwestern Telephone Company occupying rooms upstairs soon afterward. Over the following decades, the building housed a men’s clothing store, the Delano Variety Store, a furniture business, the Comet Theater, and Dr. F. R. Shanahan’s dental practice. By the 1930s it was home to the Boyce Funeral Home, and in 1941 Jack Schumacher purchased the property, remodeled the storefront, and moved his Jack Sprat grocery store there. The business later became Jack’s Food Guild, remaining until Schumacher’s retirement in the mid-1970s. The space eventually became part of Coast to Coast Hardware and today forms part of the Jerome Event Center, continuing the Brick Block’s long role in Delano’s downtown commercial life.

In February of 1905 it was announced that a solid brick block would be built on Bridge Street by Olof Peterson, Henry and Louis Bock, and J. L. Stein. J.L. Stein purchased the lot cornering on the alley and Bridge Street, where a blacksmith shop stood for years, and had the old landmark torn down to make room for his new block. The building was completed in 8 months. J.L. Stein’s was the west 25 x 90 bend of the building.

The Northwestern Telephone Co. decided to locate in the rooms above Stein’s new building in June of 1906; the erection of the brick block had just completed when John L. Stein died in October of 1906.

Leo J. Plattner opened a Gents Furnishing and Clothing Store in the Stein building in 1907, sold out in 1909, when Holmberg & Co. rented it. Later that year Bernard Blomquist opened the Delano Variety Store in Mrs. Stein’s building. Blomquist changed to being a furniture dealer, but remained in that location until 1915, when the Comet Theater moved into the west end of the brick block.

Dr. F. R. Shanahan, dentist, opened a dental parlor in the old Commercial Club rooms in the Brick Block in 1919, and he and his wife moved into one of Mrs. Stein’s apartments in the Brick Block in 1921.

Mrs. J. L. Stein died in 1939. The Boyce Funeral Home was in the building in the 1930’s, moving out when Jack Schumacher bought the building from the Stein Estate in 1941. He put on a new front, featuring large display windows, and moved his Jack Sprat grocery store from around the corner. The store became a Food Guild Store in 1951, known as Jack’s Food Guild. Jack retired in the mid 1970’s.

This is a photo taken in the late 1970’s. There is no sign on the west end of the brick block. The space eventually became part of the Coast to Coast Hardware store, and today is part of the Jerome Event Center.
